title: Lecture 12. Sociological (population) surveys of representatives of risk groups
summary:
=== 12. Sociological (Population) Surveys of Risk Group Representatives ===

1 Why Surveys Are Needed

2 Problems in Sample Formation

3 Problems in Questionnaire Formulation

4 Theoretical Model of the Survey

1. Why Surveys Are Needed When we talk about the prevention of something, for example, drug addiction, we face seemingly simple questions: exactly which and how many narcotic substances are consumed in the country? And how many drug users are there in the country? State statistics contain a lot of information about drug-addicted patients, about drug-related crimes… but answering these questions is not so simple. Why?

Because there are different categories of drug users: those who tried once a long time ago, those who use something occasionally with long breaks, there are systematic users, there are truly drug-dependent individuals... All these completely different categories consume completely different drugs, from completely different social groups: from street prostitutes to top managers of large companies. Naturally, statistics do not include any of this. And it is impossible to obtain such information from statistics because it is based on clinical and criminal samples, i.e., on accounting for individuals who fall within the purview of the healthcare system or law enforcement agencies. But there are categories of drug users who do not fall into anyone's attention, except perhaps specialized public organizations.

Such information can only be obtained by asking relevant questions to representatives of different social groups. Therefore, the only suitable tool for studying a population sample is a population or sociological survey.

2. Problems in Sample Formation The key question for any sociological study is the sample. And here, everything depends on which part of the population we want to study. Accordingly, the sample should represent this part of the population. This could be the entire population of a territory, youth, students, specific risk groups... At the same time, it is irrational to raise the question of assessing rare phenomena, such as, for example, the prevalence of drugs in society as a whole, because in the general population, it will be vanishingly small. Therefore, risk groups are surveyed, the most general of which for this problem can be identified as youth in general. And even for studying more general issues of psychological health, society is usually divided into age groups, singling out young age for separate studies, as it represents the greatest interest from the perspective of public health protection tasks.

The next question everyone asks is: how large should the sample be? This question is answered by a procedure called representation. This means that the sample structure, across all key indicators, reproduces the structure of the part of the population (general population) that we want to study. If this condition is met, then based on empirical measurements of variations in behavioral manifestations, it is considered that a sufficient sample size for all main types of behavior is 2000 people. It is completely irrelevant what territory we are studying – a municipal district or the entire world; in any case, it is sufficient to survey 2000 people. That is, increasing the sample size will not change the result. But if we need to compare two territories, for example, the situation in two regions of the country, then we will have to represent them separately, which means that the sample in each of them should be 2000 people.

All of this speaks to the extreme importance of the representation procedure. Loss of control over sample planning and execution can devalue the results of even the most extensive studies.

In practice, within the education system, due to access to the target audience — students — simplified sample formation procedures are often used. The simplest of these is a complete sample, meaning when all students in a class, school, or territory are simply surveyed. But even then, there will inevitably be a certain proportion of dropouts from the study (sick, late, truants...). And, as a rule, those who should participate in the study first and foremost are precisely the ones who drop out of the sample. They will try to evade the study, especially when they know its topic (no matter what it is). And this will inevitably lead to distorted results, which is why good studies separately analyze dropouts and assess the degree of result distortion.

Another common strategy for simplifying the sample formation procedure is the method of extreme groups. This is, for example, when in a certain territory, the most prosperous and most disadvantaged areas are selected by expert judgment, from the perspective of the research topic. Then, within these areas, the most prosperous and disadvantaged schools are selected. And within them, classes are selected based on the same principle. While this approach does not guarantee a reliable result, it provides an understanding of the spread of the behavioral traits being studied, and is generally recognized as an acceptable method for sample formation.

3. Problems in Questionnaire Formulation A questionnaire, survey form, or survey instrument is the stimulus material to which a respondent replies during a survey. Here, we will focus only on the problem of scale selection.

We can formulate all questions ourselves. But, firstly, this requires significant qualification and experience, and secondly, the research results will most likely be incomparable with the results of other studies on similar topics. And without such comparisons, it is often difficult to interpret the obtained results when we ask questions like: is this a lot or a little? Compared to whom? etc. Therefore, researchers usually try to include questions or entire blocks of questions from other similar, widely known studies in their questionnaires.

For important topics, such as youth health, there are internationally recognized methodologies that are centrally used at the national level in many countries for standardization purposes. Examples of such universally recognized international research projects for studying health status and the prevalence of various types of deviance among youth include the following:

Health Behaviour in School-Aged Children (HBSC, https://hbsc.org ↗ ), The European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs (ESPAD, https://www.espad.org), ↗ Monitoring the Future (https://monitoringthefuture.org), ↗ Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System (YRBSS, https://www.cdc.gov/yrbs) ↗ and others. These methodologies are not just questionnaires; they are fully described, strictly regulated procedures that include: ethical requirements, sample formation rules, respondent safety requirements, survey organization requirements, data processing, storage, and transfer. Countries officially participating in these projects sign relevant agreements and undertake to comply with all these rules. As a result, research findings are collected into a single database, where they undergo further in-depth processing (meta-analysis) by various specialists. In essence, entire collaborations of various research teams from different countries are built around these projects, where each team performs tasks according to its specialization.

4. Theoretical Model of the Survey At the core of a survey, like any other study, lies a theoretical model. It is based on establishing the relationship between a problem and its factors. The survey then follows the following logic for processing results. Answers to questions about the problem, for example, about drug use experience (resulting variable), allow for the identification of a risk group — questionnaires of respondents who answered affirmatively to the question about having such experience. These questionnaires can then be compared with those of respondents who answered negatively. They can be compared across all other indicators contained in the questionnaire (factorial variables). Thus, the risk group identified through questions about the problem can be described in sufficient detail. An example of such a description can be found, for instance, in the article Psychological characteristics of student youth with drug use experience / R. G. Dubrovsky // Narcology. – 2020. – Vol. 19, No. 11. – P. 59-71.
